newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Little data but markets may be edgy.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Little data but markets may be edgy.

text.p: Financial markets will ease into year-end with only a smattering of economic releases, but with stock and bond markets still ebbing and flowing economists on Friday said volatile sessions were still possible.
"I don't think you can assume the volatility will collapse in all markets just because we don't have a lot of data out," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.
Japanese inflation and unemployment figures feature prominantly in the week ahead, as do U.S. durable goods orders and French consumer spending, they said.
But with liquidity thin, analysts saw scope for choppy markets. The rapid collapse and subsequent recovery in U.S. equity prices underlined this point, they said.

"I would guess we're in the clear until early in the new year," said Paul Horne, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris. But he did not rule out the chance of exaggerated movements in stock and bond markets.

For the trendsetting U.S., November durable goods orders were the main feature. Analysts at Nomura International said they were at the low end of the forecast range with a prediction for a 1.5 percent fall in orders.
"But all we see are downside risks to our forecast, especially in aircraft and motor vehicles, which could well be weaker than our guesses," they said in a note to clients.
Analysts routinely point out that this data series can be more volatile than others.
"If there is a rebound there, there may be a little bit of concern about the economy picking up," Marshall said.

Concerns that the U.S. economy was expanding at too fast a pace have been a dominant theme for months, and any signs that the Federal Reserve might need to step on the brakes have led to large market moves, often hurting bond prices.
The week begins with U.S. personal income and spending data for November, although economists said much of that is already discounted following recent U.S. retail sales numbers.

In Japan, leading indicators are due on Tuesday, followed by industrial production, retail sales and housing starts on Thursday, and unemployment on Friday. But Marshall and others doubted the numbers would lead to a big shift in interest rate sentiment there. He said that given the current lack of liquidity, there was room for another dollar spurt as the U.S. currency often rallies at this time of year.
"The markets are very thin and it's not unusual to see quite a strong dollar." Horne at Smith Barney said French consumer spending figures, due on Friday, may be significant.
"The fourth quarter in France is starting to shape up as a problem," he said. "Any weakness in consumer spending in November would have an immediate impact on output and GDP in France."
